Current gas turbine engines operate at pressure ratios up to 25:1 and turbine inlet temperatures up to 1600 K (2400°F).
Cycle study results indicate further fuel savings can be achieved by increasing pressure ratios up to 64:1 and turbine inlet temperatures over 1650 K (2500°F).
Metal temperature prediction uncertainties of up to 100 K (180°F) are commonly encountered, leading to an iterative design process and 'overcooling' to ensure reliability.
A 2D modeling program has been developed to predict temperatures in a reacting flow field with reasonable qualitative agreement.
An interactive numerical model is being developed to predict temperature profiles downstream of dilution jet holes in combustors.
Experiments in a return loop tunnel are being used to develop empirical representations of boundary layer transition length characteristics.
Experiments on film cooling effectiveness have shown a sharp discontinuity in Stanton number where curvature begins in the flow path.
Laser anemometer measurements in turbine blade passages are being compared to 3D computational codes, with the Denton inviscid code performing the best.
Experiments on multi-pass coolant tubes have shown dramatic spikes in heat transfer at 180° bends compared to fully developed flow.
Experiments on pin fin geometries have shown much lower heat transfer coefficients for short L/D pins compared to long L/D rods.
